opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting questions right now, and honestly I don't think anyone has a fully settled answer. The way I see it, these two things started from quite different places. Search is fundamentally about retrieval: there's this enormous body of information out there, and the job is to find the most relevant pieces and point you to them, quickly and reliably. Language models started from a different angle, which is learning to model and generate language, and then it turned out that, with enough scale and the right training, they could reason a bit, synthesize, hold a conversation, follow up on what you meant rather than just what you typed.

What's happening now is that the two are converging. A pure language model on its own has real limitations. Its knowledge is frozen at training time, it can be confidently wrong, and it doesn't naturally tell you where something came from. Search is very good at exactly those things: freshness, grounding, attribution. So it feels very natural to me that the model becomes the interface, the thing that understands your intent and can do multi-step reasoning, while retrieval becomes one of the tools it uses to ground what it says in up-to-date, verifiable information.

I also think the kinds of queries people bring will shift. Many searches today are short because people have learned to talk to a search box in keywords. When you give them something conversational, they start asking much richer, more complex questions, things that would previously have taken ten searches and a lot of reading. That's where these systems really add value. For a lot of quick factual lookups, the classic experience is still great, and I don't think that goes away overnight.

So rather than one replacing the other, I see more of a blending. The model brings understanding and synthesis, search brings breadth and grounding, and the open research question is how to make that combination truly reliable, so people can trust the answer and still dig into the sources when they want to.

r001.rationale: The response says retrieval can be a tool the model uses to ground answers in current, verifiable information.

r002.rationale: It describes the model using search and says the two are converging, but does not clearly say traditional Search is incorporating language-model capabilities into its own experience.

r003.rationale: The response says no one has a fully settled answer and frames the future as blending rather than one replacing the other.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're converging more than people expect, but they're not the same product, and I don't think one simply replaces the other.

Search, at its core, is about retrieval. You have a query, you have an index of the world's information, and you want to surface the most relevant documents. It's extremely good at that, it's fast, it's cheap, and critically it's grounded: the answer points to a source that exists. LLMs are a different kind of object. They've compressed a huge amount of that same information into their weights, and they can synthesize, reason, and talk to you about it in a way that a ranked list of links never could. But that compression is lossy. The model doesn't know what happened yesterday, and it can be confidently wrong.

So the obvious thing, and what you're already seeing everywhere, is to combine them. The model becomes the interface and the reasoning layer, and search becomes a tool the model calls to ground itself. You ask something, the model decides whether it needs fresh or specific information, goes and retrieves it, reads it, and then gives you an answer with citations. That's a much better experience for a lot of queries than either piece alone. And I think a lot of the "hallucination" debate goes away once the model is reading real documents rather than reciting from memory.

Where I think it gets interesting is which queries go where. If I want the website for a restaurant, I don't want a paragraph, I want the link. Navigation-style queries are probably going to stay search-like for a long time. If I want to understand a topic, compare options, or do something multi-step, the chat interface wins, because it's conversational and I can refine. And then there's a third category that neither old search nor a chatbot really handled: tasks. Not "find me information about flights" but "book me the flight." That's where agents come in, and I think that's actually the bigger shift. Search answered questions, chat answers questions better, agents start doing things.

The other thing I'd flag is the economics and the ecosystem. Search sent traffic to the web, and that funded the web. If the model just gives you the answer, that loop changes, and I don't think anyone has fully worked out what the new equilibrium looks like. Citations help, but it's a real open question.

So, long term: I'd bet the distinction blurs to the point where users don't think about it. You'll just ask, and the system will decide how much to retrieve, how much to reason, and whether to go act on your behalf. Search doesn't die, it becomes infrastructure underneath something more capable.

r001.rationale: It says the model can call search to retrieve and read current or specific information, then use it to ground its answer.

r002.rationale: It describes the model as the interface and search as its tool, but does not describe traditional Search adding language-model capabilities to its own experience.

r003.rationale: It says neither product simply replaces the other and that the distinction may blur, but does not clearly state uncertainty about which will dominate.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Search is a way of accessing information, and a language model gives you a different interface to that information. You can ask a question, clarify what you meant, and have a conversation rather than formulate a query and then go through links yourself.

But the model still needs access to information that’s current, and you often want to know where an answer came from. So I don’t think it’s simply that a chatbot replaces Search. I think you’ll see systems that bring the two together: the model can search when it needs to, use what it finds, and help you make sense of it.

The interesting question is how much work the system can do for you while keeping you able to check the answer. For some questions, you want a quick response. For others, exploring the sources is really the point. I think there’s room for both.

r001.rationale: It says the model can search when needed, use what it finds, and help make sense of it.

r002.rationale: The response describes a chatbot using Search, but does not say traditional Search will incorporate language-model capabilities into its own experience.

r003.rationale: It says chatbots do not simply replace Search and that there is room for both, but does not state that it is currently unclear which will dominate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re going to converge in some ways. Search is very good at finding information, and language models give you a different way to interact with that information. You can ask a question, get an explanation, ask a follow-up, and keep refining what you’re trying to understand.

But a chatbot still needs access to information that’s current, and you often want to see the source. So I don’t see this as simply replacing search with something that generates an answer from memory. There’s a lot of value in combining retrieval with the ability to reason over what you retrieve and present it in a useful way.

The right interface probably depends on the task. Sometimes you want a quick answer. Sometimes you want to explore, compare sources, or go directly to a website. I think we’ll see systems that move more fluidly between those modes.

r001.rationale: The response says chatbots need current information and describes combining retrieval with language models’ ability to reason over and present that information.

r002.rationale: It describes combining search and language-model capabilities, but does not clearly say traditional Search will incorporate those capabilities into its own experience.

r003.rationale: The response predicts convergence and says the interface depends on the task, but does not state that it is unclear which will dominate.
